title: Why you replay embarrassing moments forever
script: Your brain replays your most embarrassing moments on loop. It treats social mistakes like threats. But here's the twist: psychologists call it the spotlight effect. Other people noticed far less than you think. Nobody remembers it like you do.
description: The spotlight effect explained in 15 seconds.

title: Why unfinished tasks haunt your brain
script: Your brain can't let go of unfinished tasks. It's called the Zeigarnik effect. An open loop keeps nagging you in the background. The fix? Write down your plan. Once it's on paper, your brain finally relaxes.
description: Why open loops drain your focus, and the simple fix.

title: The popcorn trick that makes you overpay
script: Ever notice the medium popcorn makes no sense? That's the decoy effect. A useless middle option exists only to make the large one look like a bargain. Spot the decoy, and you stop overpaying.
description: The decoy effect in everyday pricing.

title: Why you see things everywhere after learning them
script: Ever learn a new word, then see it everywhere? That's the frequency illusion. It isn't appearing more often. Your brain just started noticing it. Attention changes what you see, not what exists.

title: You remember the ending, not the whole experience
script: You don't remember experiences as an average. You remember the peak and the ending. It's called the peak-end rule. A great finish can rescue a boring day. So always end strong.

title: Why you love things you build yourself
script: People value things more when they build them themselves. It's called the IKEA effect. Even a wobbly shelf feels special if your own hands made it. Effort creates love.

title: Why beginners feel so confident
script: The less you know about something, the more confident you often feel. That's the Dunning-Kruger effect. Beginners can't yet see what they're missing. Real experts tend to doubt themselves more.

title: Why you start liking songs you hated
script: You like things more just because you've seen them often. It's the mere exposure effect. Familiarity feels like safety to your brain. That's why an annoying song slowly becomes your favorite.

title: Why you stay in things that aren't working
script: You finish a bad movie because you already paid for it. That's the sunk cost fallacy. The money is gone either way. Ask yourself one question: what's best from here?
description: The sunk cost fallacy in everyday life.

title: Want someone to like you? Ask for a favor
script: Want someone to like you? Ask them for a small favor. It's called the Ben Franklin effect. When people help you, their brain explains it by deciding they must like you. Favors build bonds.

title: Why new things stop feeling exciting
script: A new phone feels amazing for a week, then it's just your phone. Psychologists call it hedonic adaptation. Your brain gets used to good things fast. So enjoy small moments before they become normal.

title: How you hear your name in a loud room
script: In a loud room, you suddenly hear your own name across the crowd. That's the cocktail party effect. Your brain filters out noise, but keeps watching for what matters to you.

title: The first number always wins
script: The first number you hear controls every number after it. It's called anchoring. A high starting price makes the next one feel cheap. In a negotiation, always make the first offer yourself.

title: Why small mistakes make you more likable
script: Making a small mistake can make you more likable. It's the pratfall effect, but only if people already see you as competent. Competence plus one tiny flaw feels human.
